3. For proper appreciation of the questions relevant facts may be stated thus: The property described in the schedule to the plaint belonged to Ismail Gazi who married five wives and died leaving a number of heirs through them. Ismail Gazi made a waqf of his property and executed a deed of waqf in respect of the property described in the deed itself. Ismail Gazi put his thumb impressions on the deed of waqf as he could not sign due to his illness and a few days after execution of the deed Ismail Gazi died on 22-4-1939 before the waqf deed could be registered and after his death heirs got the waqfnama registered. Hashem Gazi, one of the sons of Ismail Gazi, got the waqf enrolled and being the eldest son became the first Mutwalli. Subsequently the appellant became the Mutwalli. There were certain property which was left out of the waqfnama but those were also recorded in the R.S. Khatian as waqf property in accordance with the wish of the wakif. For dealing with the excess land a miscellaneous case being Miscellaneous Case No. 10 of 1952 was started by the Revenue Officer under section 20 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and out of 81. 81 acres of land in khas possession of the appellant as the Mutwalli and in his personal capacity a total quantity of 36.06 acres including homestead was allotted to him and the remaining 45.75 acres of land was declared excess under section 20 of the Act; and the excess land was acquired by the Government. The mutwalli prayed for release of the excess land upon which Case No. 16 of 1961-62 was started by the authorities, and out of 45.75 acres order was passed for release of 22.46 acres in his favour, and the balance 23.29 acres of land were not released. Hence the suit was filed by the appellant for a declaration as indicated above. The suit was contested by the Province of East Pakistan by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the plaintiff was found in possession of 81.81 acres out of which 76.86 acres were covered by the waqf and 4.95 acres were outside the waqf. The plaintiff according to the existing provisions of law is entitled to retain 33.33 acres of land from the waqf estate and 4.94 acres from his personal estate and the homestead; and the plaintiff has been allotted 36.06 acres in Miscellaneous Case No. 10/52 under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of Camp Jharakhali J.L. No. 45/80 P.S. Amtali, and rest of the excess land, that is 33.29 acres has been acquired by the Government and the same was settled with different persons. Defendants Nos. 2 to 5 claiming to be lawful heirs of Ismail Gazi after getting themselves added as defendants contested the suit. They denied the plaintiff's case about the creation of the waqf by Ismail Gazi and contended inter alia that the waqfnama is vague, fabricated and antedated and fraudulent document which was not excused by Ismail Gazi. Their case is that Ismail Gazi was confined to bed for a long time till his death and be was unconscious for several days before he breathed last. They alleged that Ismail Gazi was literate and there was no need for him to put thumb impression. They claim to be in possession of the property as Ismail Gazi's legal heirs and according to their legal shares. 

 6. From the judgment it appears that at the hearing of the appeals, for the first time it was contended by the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants in First Appeal No.83 of 1967 that in the absence of any stipulation in the waqfnama the ultimate benefit for religious and charitable purpose, the waqfnama being in contravention of the provisions of the Mussalman Waqf Validating Act, 1993, the waqf is invalid and as such the plaintiff is not entitled to get the declaration as prayed for." On examining the different clauses of the waqfnama the learned Judges observed that "no where it was stated that the ultimate benefit' will be for religious, charitable purpose could be found". According to the learned Judges there is no mention of the vesting of the ultimate benefit in charity nor there is any implied gift to charity. According to them waqfnama cannot stand the test or law, as it merely sets out a family arrangement binding the property in perpetuity for the benefit and enjoyment of the heirs of the so called wakif in arriving at this conclusion, the learned Judges referred to the decisions of the Dacca High Court in the cases of Mst. Khairunnessa Khatun Chowdhury v. Golam Muktadir Chowdhury, 14 DLR 745 and Syed Abu Fazal v. Syeda Sayeeda Khatun and others, 15 DLR 163. 

 8. On close examination of the different clauses of the waqfnama I find there is substance in the above contention. The waqfnama does not appear to have been correctly construed and this led the learned Judges to come to an erroneous decision. The Preamble of the waqfnama name clearly shows that all the properties owned by Ismail Gazi Howlader were permanently dedicated in the way of Allah and the waqfnama as the supporting document would remain operative for all time to come and the waqf estate would continue permanently. So the dedication as permanent.Relevant portion of the preamble is quoted below: 

 9. One of the requirements of a valid waqfnama is that the dedication of the property must be in the way of Allah and it must be permanent. The preamble of the waqfnama in my opinion sufficiently complies with the requirement. The manner of use of the waqf property as delineated in the different clauses of the waqfnama also shows that the wakif made clear provisions to ensure complete dedication in accordance with' the requirement of Muslim law. Clauses 1 to 6 provide for payment of allowance to different beneficiaries named in the waqfnama, Clause 7 provides that Rs. 10/- to be spent annually for religious purpose in the name of Allah out of the fund of the waqf estate. Clause 14 contains the provision to meet an unforeseen situation in the event of absence of any male member among his descendants. Clause 14 sufficiently ensures that In such a case the management of the waqf estate shall be carried on by any one of his near relations who is of good character and pious. Clause 14 reads as under:- 

 10. The waqfnama does not suffer from any vagueness; it is a complete dedication of all the property owned by the wakif. It contains a provision to the effect that if it transpires that any of his property has been omitted while describing in the schedules that also shall be treated as part of the waqf estate. The waqfnama ensures- 

 (5)that a specified amount out of the income of the waqf estate, though small, is to be spent on public charity; 

 (6) that the management of the waqf estate must continue even in the event of absence of any male member among his descendants. 

 12. In the instant case in the waqfnama the beneficiaries have been specified, with a declaration that excepting the named beneficiaries there shall not be any beneficiary. In the case of death of a son without any issue, his widow shall not get any share in the waqf estate. The waqfnama contains a provision that even a son may have his right to the allowance forfeited in the event of his going away elsewhere. In the event of total extinction of the beneficiaries named in the waqfnama, obviously, only consequence that would follow is that the waqf becomes "lillah" and the entire income goes to the poor and charitable purposes. So, in this case me ultimate benefit for the poor or a religious, pious or charitable purpose of a permanent character, has been impliedly reserved. This implied reservation is sufficient compliance of the law. 

 14. Waqf means permanent dedication by a person professing Mussalman faith of any property owned by him for any purpose recognized by the Mussalman law as religious, pious or charitable. This is the definition of waqf as given in Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913. The definition practically gives recognition to the opinion of Imam Abu Hanifa. According to his opinion waqf is the detention of a specific thing in the ownership of the wakif or appropriator, and the devoting or appropriating of its profits or usufruct in charity on the poor or other good objects, "and this was elucidated by Abu Yusuf and Muhammed, the two great disciples of Imam Abu Hanifa. According to them, waqf signifies the extinction of the appropriator's ownership in the thing dedicated and the detention of the thing in the implied ownership of Allah, in such a manner that its profits may revert to or be applied for the benefit of the mankind". Thus a Waqf extinguishes the right of the waqf in the property dedicated and transfers impliedly to Allah. The mutwalli is merely the manager of the waqf estate, but the property does not vest in him as in the case of a trust, under the Trust Act. 

 17. The learned Judges invalidated the waqfnama which has been acted upon, and which was recognised by the Government in dealing with the waqf property. The judgment does not show that the learned Judges considered the effect of operation of clause 14 of the Waqfnama in the event of absence of any male member in the line of wakif's succession. In such an event the management of the waqf estate goes outside the family. This provision alone in my opinion is sufficient to indicate the object of the wakif that the waqf would continue in perpetuity even in the absence of his male heirs. Once the management of the waqf estate goes outside the family of the wakif, it ceases for all practical purposes to be a private waqf that is Waqf-al-Awlad. From the very fact that the dedication is perpetual and there is a provision continuance of the waqf estate in the event of absence of any male member in the line of waqif descendants the waqfnama must be construed to have created a valid waqf in accordance with the Mussalman Waqf Validating Act, 1913. In my opinion the waqfnama has not been correctly construed by the learned Judges, and on this ground the judgment of the High Court must be set aside. The learned Judges while affirming the findings of the trial Court, that the waqfnama was a genuine document; it was duly executed by Ismail Gazi Howlader; and it was acted upon, set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court on view of invalidity of the waqfnama, which was not agitated before the trial Court. The learned Judges dismissed the suit only on this ground.
